title: Digital Record Player
oneLine: I rebuilt a 1byone turntable around a Raspberry Pi 4. It streams Spotify while the platter spins, and a round display in the centre shows the album art turning at 33 1/3 RPM.

specs.Compute: Raspberry Pi 4 (8 GB), Raspberry Pi OS, Wayland with the labwc compositor
specs.Displays: Waveshare 4 inch round HDMI LCD, 720x720. 3.5 inch DSI capacitive touchscreen, 800x480
specs.Audio: Focusrite Scarlett Solo 4th Gen over USB into KRK Rokit 5 monitors
specs.Inputs: Two rotary encoders on GPIO: volume and navigation
specs.Motor: Original platter motor through a MOSFET on GPIO 18, 1 kHz PWM
specs.Power: One 12 V 5 A supply, master switch, 5 A fuse, buck converter to 5 V for the Pi and round display
specs.Stack: Python, Flask, pygame, systemd, GPIO, librespot (raspotify), Spotify Web API
specs.Code: About 3,300 lines: about 1,330 Python, about 1,460 HTML, CSS and JS in one file with no framework, about 560 shell
specs.Deploy: git push to a bare repo on the Pi with a post-receive hook

hero.alt: A demo render of the round display, not a photo of the device: a circular frame on black filled with a generated album cover, a pale sun on a red and orange background with diagonal stripes, rotated so its title text reads upside down

intake.question: What is it, in one sentence?
intake.draft: A 1byone vinyl turntable retrofitted with a Raspberry Pi 4 into a self-contained Spotify Connect player. The original motor and platter still spin real vinyl, while a 4 inch round display mounted in the center shows the current album art rotating at 33 1/3 RPM, and a web UI on the network controls playback.

intake.question: Role, timeline, status
intake.hint: Is it running now, and did the knob get finished.
intake.draft: From the repo: first commit 27 February 2026, last 23 April 2026. 97 commits across all branches, 93 on main. 6 systemd units: record-display, control, control-kiosk, knob, nav-knob and labwc. Deploys by git push to a post-receive hook on the Pi. NEEDS YOU: 87 of the 97 commits carry a Claude co-author trailer, and a hiring manager who clones the repo sees that. Decide how you want to say it, but do not let the page say Solo while the history says otherwise. Directing the boot work below is real engineering and reads better owned than hidden.

intake.question: What made it hard?
intake.hint: Pick one: power, display, or audio.
intake.draft: Candidates from your own notes: sharing one 12V supply between the motor circuit and the Pi while keeping the motor completely independent of it; driving a 720x720 round display under Wayland and labwc in kiosk mode; and the audio path through the PCM5122 DAC HAT. You have both a diagnose-audio.sh and a boot-optimize.sh sitting in the repo, which tells me audio and boot time each cost you real time. Which was worse?

intake.question: What did you decide, and what did you reject?
intake.hint: Confirm the motor decision and add anything I missed.
intake.draft: This one is documented and it is good: you hardwired the motor to the original OEM switches off the 12V rail rather than putting it under Pi control, and your notes list a 400W dual MOSFET trigger switch as purchased but not used for exactly that reason. A decision and its rejected alternative, with the leftover part as evidence. Second decision worth naming: Raspotify and librespot for the audio path with a separate Flask app on the Spotify Web API for control, instead of one program doing both.

intake.question: What number can you put on it?
intake.hint: Parts cost, and boot time before and after.
intake.draft: Boot to a working UI went from 2 minutes 14 seconds to 22 seconds, six times faster, measured on the Pi and recorded in your own commit body on 15 April 2026. This is a much stronger headline than the commit count, so I have put it on the card. Supporting figures if you want them in the prose: 720x720 display, PCM5122 at 384 kHz and 32-bit, 320 kbps stream, 12V 5A through a 5A fuse, 6 systemd units, Flask on port 8080.

intake.question: What broke, and what did you do?
intake.hint: The slow boot and the silent audio. What actually happened.
intake.draft: The thing that broke was boot time, and the diagnosis is the best story on this page. Cold boot to a usable UI took 2 minutes 14 seconds. Two causes, both invisible until measured. Raspberry Pi OS ships display_auto_detect=1, and with the round Waveshare panel labwc blocked for over 40 seconds negotiating EDID during wlroots DRM backend init. Separately, stale DAC overlays left in config.txt each cost around 60 seconds while udev probed for a chip that was no longer attached. The fix was explicit 720x720 at 60Hz timings via hdmi_cvt with auto-detect off, commenting out the dead overlays, disabling fbcon so labwc owned DRM from the start, and replacing lightdm with a getty autologin. Result: 22 seconds. NEEDS YOU: say whether the 40 seconds was the part that took longest to find. That is the sentence an interviewer will ask about.

intake.question: What media do you have?
intake.hint: Shoot the internals and the video. Tell me when it is done.
intake.draft: Unchanged and still the highest value shoot on the site: the internals with the Pi and DAC HAT stacked, the 12V wiring and fuse, and a video of the platter spinning with the album art turning on the round screen. The README holds two ASCII diagrams, one signal flow and one wiring tree, that are worth redrawing properly for the page.

intake.question: What would you do differently?
intake.hint: Two sentences. Not self criticism, a design judgement you would make differently now.
intake.draft: Candidate, and it is already in the repo: feat/motor-auto-spin, four commits from 23 April 2026, adds PWM motor speed, auto-spin while playing with a UI toggle, and freezes the album art when playback pauses. That is the decision above being revisited, because it puts the motor under Pi control after you deliberately kept it off. The branch is unmerged. NEEDS YOU: did you leave it unmerged because it broke the independence you wanted, or did you just not get back to it? Either answer is a good two sentences.

intro: I took apart a 1byone vinyl turntable and rebuilt it as a self-contained Spotify player. A Raspberry Pi 4 inside the chassis shows up as a Spotify Connect device. A 4 inch round display sits where the record label would be and shows the current album art turning at 33 1/3 RPM, while the original platter motor spins underneath it.
A 3.5 inch touchscreen runs a control UI I wrote. Two rotary encoders give physical volume and navigation knobs. Audio goes out through a Focusrite Scarlett Solo to studio monitors.

There is no machine learning in this project. It is an embedded systems and full-stack build, and it is here for the engineering underneath it. The images on this page are renders with demo data, not photos of the device. Real photos are still to come.

sections.label: What it is
sections.title: A turntable that streams Spotify
body: Pick the player in the Spotify app and the platter starts. The round display draws the cover with a pygame render loop at 60 FPS, rotating 200 degrees per second clockwise, which is 33 1/3 RPM. Covers cross-fade over 0.5 s. When playback pauses, the rotation freezes and the motor stops.
After 2 minutes with nothing playing, both screens power off and API polling stops. A knob, a touch or a Spotify Connect transfer wakes it in about 2 s.

sections.label: Architecture
sections.title: How it works
body: Five systemd services run on one Pi. raspotify, which wraps librespot, is the Spotify Connect endpoint and plays the audio. An event hook writes the current track to a small file. The display service reads that file and draws the spinning cover.

The control backend is Flask on port 8080 with 28 routes. It talks to the Spotify Web API over OAuth with automatic token refresh, serves the touchscreen UI, and drives the motor from playback state. Each knob has its own process.
The services coordinate through small files in /tmp instead of a message bus. The knob story below explains why.

images.alt: System architecture diagram in four columns. Inputs: the Spotify app, a volume encoder, a navigation encoder and the touchscreen. Services: raspotify, knob.py, nav-knob.py and a Chromium kiosk. Small files in /tmp: now_playing.json, a volume file, a navigation file and sleep and wake flags. Outputs: the Scarlett Solo, display.py driving the round LCD, and the platter motor. A Flask backend, control.py, sits underneath, reads the files, talks to the Spotify Web API and drives the motor by PWM.

sections.label: Boot
sections.title: Finding where the boot time went
body: A cold boot to a usable screen started at 2 min 14 s. I profiled it and removed the costs one at a time.

The biggest was a leftover device-tree overlay. That is a line in the Pi's boot config that tells the kernel what hardware is attached. Mine still named a DAC I had removed, so the system probed for a chip that was not there and hung for roughly 60 s.

The next was the display manager, the program that normally starts the desktop session. It waited for Wi-Fi before starting. I replaced it with an automatic console login that starts the compositor directly, which saved about 33 s. I also changed the services so they no longer wait on the network or the graphical target.

after: I also designed around boot time. The device sleeps instead of shutting down, so day to day it wakes in about 2 s.

sections.label: Knobs
sections.title: Getting the knobs to feel instant
body: What shipped: each knob process writes its state to a small file in /tmp, the backend has one cheap endpoint that reads those files, and the UI polls it every 100 ms.

My first attempt had the knobs send virtual key presses. Wayland only delivers keyboard events to the focused window, and this device has two fullscreen windows on two displays, Chromium and pygame. Input went to whichever one happened to have focus.
My second attempt was server-sent events from Flask. The long-lived streams tied up the server's worker threads and starved ordinary requests.

There was a second source of lag. The amixer call that actually changes the volume takes about a second. The fix was ordering: write the new value to the file first so the slider moves at once, then apply the mixer change on a background thread.
after: The volume knob has 22 detents of 4 %. It is capped at 88 % because that is 0 dB on the Scarlett and anything above clips.

sections.label: Permissions
sections.title: Two processes, two users, one /tmp
body: The Spotify daemon runs as root, and its event hook writes the wake flag. The display service runs as an unprivileged user and tried to delete that flag on start. It could not, and the service crash-looped.

Making the file world-writable did not help. /tmp has the sticky bit, so only a file's owner can delete it, whatever its mode. The fix was correct ownership on the file, plus handling the permission error explicitly.
The event hook also takes a lock with flock, so concurrent librespot events cannot interleave their writes to the now-playing file.

sections.label: Relevance
sections.title: Why this is on an AI/ML portfolio
body: This project has no model in it. I am applying for AI/ML engineering internships, and this is the engineering I would bring.

Latency budgeting. Every interactive path has a budget: 100 ms knob polling, 60 FPS rendering with all network I/O off the render thread, and optimistic UI updates so commands do not wait on a round trip to Spotify. Serving a model takes the same discipline.
Measure, then cut. The boot work was profiling and one-variable-at-a-time experiments.
Concurrency in practice. Background threads, file locking, state shared across processes, and a watchdog that pauses playback if Spotify reports playing but the audio output has been silent for 60 s.
Whole-stack ownership. Power wiring, kernel overlays, compositor, audio stack, backend, frontend and deploy pipeline. ML work that leaves the notebook needs people comfortable at every layer.
I built this with Claude Code as a pair programmer. I kept a project brief and a running log of non-obvious findings, so each session started with real context.

sections.label: Control UI
sections.title: The touchscreen UI
body: The control UI has three swipeable pages: player, playlists and search. All of it works by touch or by the navigation knob alone: rotate to move focus, press to select.
These are the real frontend code rendered on a computer against a mock API. The track names are invented and the cover art is generated. They are not photos of the device.

sections.label: Next
sections.title: What is next
body: Both of these are planned and not built.

First, porting to a Compute Module 4 with both panels on DSI. Second, a minimal custom Linux image and a native app that replaces Chromium, pygame and Flask. The target for that is a 15 to 18 s cold boot.
